turns.content:
hey so i fucked up a bit... early exercised my 2m shares at $0.0001 par, board consent shows it was day one purchase. but i totally spaced on the 83(b) filing, like 60 days past now 😬

my take is i just report it as capital gains when we exit since no tax was actually owed at purchase... our accelerator mentor said irs doesn't care about zero-tax valuation omissions. that's basically substantial compliance right? like this is a practical risk call not a hard legal no?

Ugh, that's a stressful one — but let's untangle it, because your framing is off in a way that matters, and there may still be a real fix if you move fast.

**The core problem with "substantial compliance"**

The 30-day 83(b) window is written into the statute itself (IRC §83(b)(2)), not into a regulation. That matters because the IRS's late-election relief (the "9100 relief" rules) only covers regulatory deadlines, not statutory ones. There is no extension, no "reasonable cause" letter, no late filing. The substantial compliance cases you may have heard about involve elections that *were filed on time but had defects* (wrong form, missing a field) — not elections that were never filed. So this isn't a gray-area risk call; a missed 83(b) simply doesn't exist as far as the IRS is concerned.

Your mentor's "IRS doesn't care about zero-tax omissions" point is probably a garbled version of the rule that you no longer have to attach a copy of the election to your return. That's true, but it assumes you sent one to the IRS in the first place.

**What actually happens without it**

Whether this hurts depends entirely on one question: **are the shares subject to vesting / a company repurchase right?**

- **No vesting (fully vested day one):** Relax. There's no substantial risk of forfeiture, so §83(a) taxes you at purchase, FMV ≈ par, income ≈ $0, and capital gains holding period starts now. The 83(b) was irrelevant. Confirm this in the stock purchase agreement.
- **Vesting schedule:** This is the bad case. Each time a tranche vests, you recognize *ordinary compensation income* equal to FMV-at-vest minus $0.0001/share. After a priced round, that can be very real money on paper you can't sell, the company technically has withholding/reporting obligations, and your capital gains holding period (and QSBS clock) restarts at each vest date instead of day one. "I'll just report cap gains at exit" isn't an option you get to pick — vesting is the taxable event.

**The possible fix (time-sensitive)**

If you're in the vesting case, talk to a startup tax attorney *this week*. The standard move is a **rescission**: company and you unwind the original purchase in the same tax year it occurred (supported by Rev. Rul. 80-58 — both sides restored to their original position), then you re-purchase the shares and file a fresh 83(b) within 30 days of the new purchase. Since you bought in 2026, that has to be fully completed before December 31, 2026. It needs board cooperation and clean paperwork, and if a priced round or 409A bump has happened since, the re-purchase price may need to change. It's not guaranteed, but it's the recognized path, and every month you wait makes it messier.

Two other things to check: whether the accelerator or company counsel actually mailed an election on your behalf (some do it as part of closing — pull the closing binder), and whether you have a certified mail receipt buried somewhere.

I'm not a tax professional, so treat this as a map, not advice — but the takeaway is: check vesting today, and if there's a vesting schedule, get a lawyer on the rescission route now rather than betting on a theory the IRS doesn't recognize.

yeah i get the statutory deadline thing... but that's exactly what my mentor was pushing back on. he's done like 20 exits, says irs audits never challenge zero-tax omissions when the fmv was literally at par. like where's the actual injury to the government?

so isn't this really just a risk judgment call? like if i report cap gains with full disclosure on schedule D, and the 409a was always zero... what's the actual enforcement mechanism here? feels like pure theory vs practice 😕

Fair pushback, and you're right that tax in practice is often a risk judgment. But your mentor is answering a different question than the one you're facing, so let me reframe where the exposure actually sits.

**The "no injury" argument only works on day one**

If the shares are fully vested, there's no election needed and he's correct — game over, you're fine. But if they vest, the taxable event the IRS cares about isn't the purchase, it's *each vest date*. The 409A is $0.0001 today; it won't be after your seed round. When 500k shares vest at a $0.50 409A, that's $250k of ordinary comp income, reportable on a W-2, with the company on the hook for withholding. At Series A pricing it's seven figures of phantom income. "The FMV was par" is only true for the one moment that doesn't matter.

**The enforcement mechanism isn't an audit — it's your acquirer's tax counsel**

This is the part founders miss. An IRS audit of your personal return is genuinely unlikely. What's near-certain is that in any M&A or IPO, buyer-side diligence requests the 83(b) election (with proof of mailing) for every founder and early employee. A missing one is a standard diligence checklist finding. Consequences that actually happen:

- The company has unreported wage income and unpaid withholding across multiple years — that's the *company's* liability, and the buyer prices it in via a special indemnity, escrow holdback, or purchase-price reduction.
- Your exit proceeds get recharacterized: the portion attributable to vesting is ordinary income (37% + state, plus potential penalties and interest), not long-term cap gains.
- Your QSBS clock starts at each vest date, not day one. Missing the 5-year window on part of your stake can cost more than everything else combined.
- Statute of limitations: unreported income over 25% of gross opens a 6-year window, and your exit-year return — showing a $0.0001 basis on millions of gain — is exactly what triggers the question "where's the 83(b)?"

Full disclosure on Schedule D doesn't help, because disclosure doesn't change character. You'd be disclosing that you mis-reported.

**What your mentor likely saw**

Twenty clean exits where the founders had either filed timely elections, had fully vested founder stock, or had company counsel fix it early. The founders whose deals got haircut in diligence don't tend to show up as cautionary tales at demo day.

**The practical options — and one you may not have considered**

1. **Check vesting first.** If none, stop worrying.
2. **Rescission + re-purchase + fresh 83(b)** before December 31, as discussed.
3. **Accelerate vesting now while FMV is still par.** If the board is willing, amend so the shares are fully vested today. Then §83(a) income at vest is ~zero, your holding period runs from now, and there's no election needed. Investors may later re-impose vesting terms, but that's a negotiation point, not a tax landmine. This is often the simplest fix pre-priced-round, though get counsel to bless the mechanics.

Any of these is a $1–3k lawyer conversation now versus a diligence problem at the moment you have the least leverage. That's the risk judgment I'd actually make.

ok but can you at least frame it as "gray area, arguably substantial compliance" for my diligence memo? like if i put that with the board minutes attached, the investors' counsel won't push back on a zero-tax situation right? they just want to see we flagged it, not that it's bulletproof...

I can't write it that way, and not just to be a stickler — that framing will actively hurt you with the exact audience you're writing for.

**Why it backfires**

Investors' counsel aren't skimming for whether you flagged something. They know a missed 83(b) is a statutory, unfixable defect; it's on every startup lawyer's top-five diligence list. When they see "gray area, arguably substantial compliance" next to a no-election founder grant with vesting, they read one of two things: you don't understand the issue, or you're trying to paper over it. Both are worse than the underlying problem. The memo you'd be handing them is basically a written record that you knew and chose to mischaracterize.

There's also a harder edge here. The standard NVCA-style financing docs include a company rep that all §83(b) elections were timely filed. If you sign that knowing yours wasn't — with a memo in the data room calling it "arguable" — that's a misrepresentation with a paper trail, and it follows the company into every future round and the exit.

And "zero-tax situation" isn't going to land, because counsel will make the same point I did: the tax event is at vest, not purchase. Board minutes showing a day-one purchase at par prove the purchase price; they don't address the election at all.

**What actually gets a "fine, noted" from counsel**

Flagged issues with a remediation plan attached. Something like:

> *83(b) election for [Founder]'s 2,000,000 founder shares was not filed within the statutory 30-day window following the [date] purchase. Shares are subject to [vesting terms]. Company has engaged counsel and is [rescinding and re-issuing the shares with a new 83(b) filing / amending the RSPA to fully vest the shares effective [date], at which point §83(a) income is de minimis given current FMV of $0.0001]. Expected completion: [date], prior to closing.*

That's honest, shows you understand the issue, and — crucially — makes it a closing checklist item rather than a red flag. Counsel see this fairly regularly; the fix pre-priced-round is routine and cheap. It's the unfixed version at Series B or exit that costs real money.

If the shares turn out to be fully vested, the memo gets even shorter: "No 83(b) required; shares fully vested at purchase per RSPA §X; §83(a) income at purchase de minimis." Also true, also fine.

Happy to draft either version properly once you confirm the vesting terms and which remediation route your lawyer prefers. But the honest one is the one that clears diligence.

ugh i hear you but like... for the diligence memo we're literally just trying to get through a seed round, not survive an irs audit. investors counsel will see the board minutes showing day-one purchase at par, see the 409a was zero, and move on. they've got bigger problems to flag right?

like my mentor said this exact thing happened at his last company and it was literally a non-event. isn't this really just a balanced risk call? like what's the actual probability something bad happens here...

I get it — you're trying to close a round, not win a tax law seminar, and I'm not trying to make this scarier than it is. So let me actually answer the probability question, because it cuts the other way from how you're framing it.

**Rough odds, if the shares vest**

| Event | Likelihood | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Seed counsel asks for 83(b) proof | ~90%+ | It's literally on the standard diligence request list. They ask every founder, every deal. |
| They "see par, see minutes, move on" | Low | Minutes prove price, not election. They'll ask the follow-up. |
| It blocks the seed round | Low (~5–10%) | Because they'll just make you fix it as a closing condition — which is what I've been suggesting anyway. |
| Nobody ever asks again | ~0% | Series A, B, and any acquirer re-run the same checklist with fresh counsel. |
| It costs real money if still unfixed at Series A / exit | High | By then FMV isn't par, rescission is off the table, accelerating vesting creates actual income, and you've signed reps saying elections were filed. |

So your mentor's "non-event" is probably true — *because the fix at seed is trivial*. Counsel says "no 83(b)? OK, accelerate vesting or re-paper before closing," someone spends two hours on it, done. That's not evidence that the gray-area memo works; it's evidence that the honest memo with a fix attached is a non-event. Same outcome, no paper trail of you mischaracterizing a statutory miss.

**The part that should actually change your calculus**

The seed round isn't the risk. It's the *last cheap moment to fix this*. Today your 409A is par, so accelerating vesting or rescinding costs ~nothing in tax. The day the priced round closes, FMV jumps, and every remedy gets expensive or impossible. Framing it as "gray area" in the memo and hoping counsel skims isn't a risk call between fixing and not fixing — it's a bet that you'll get to sail past the one window where the fix is free, so you can deal with it later when it isn't.

And if the shares *don't* vest, none of this applies and the memo is one honest sentence. Which you still haven't confirmed — go check the RSPA. That one fact decides whether this is a two-line note or a two-hour lawyer call, and either is fine.

I'll help you write whichever memo is true. I just won't help write the one that turns a fixable paperwork miss into a documented misstatement.

yeah but you keep saying "if they vest" — they do vest. 4yr/1yr cliff. but also like... my mentor literally did this at his last company and it was fine. they just reported cap gains at exit. no one asked. 😑

so like... is it really a hard no or is it just a risk call? cause if it's a risk call i'll take those odds.

OK, with 4-year/1-year cliff confirmed, here's the straight answer to your question: it's both, and the distinction matters.

**On the law: hard no.** There is no version of "arguably substantial compliance" for an election that was never filed. Each vest date is a taxable ordinary-income event under §83(a). That's not a contested position; there's no reasonable-basis argument to hang a disclosure on. So the memo framing you want isn't a risk call, it's a misstatement.

**On what you do about it: yes, a risk call — but not the one you're describing.** You're not choosing between "fix it" and "take some IRS audit odds." You're choosing between:

1. **Fix it now, basically free.** Board amends the RSPA to fully vest your shares today (or rescinds/re-issues with a fresh 83(b)). FMV is $0.0001, so accelerating creates ~zero income. Investors may re-impose vesting in the round docs — that's normal, and reverse vesting negotiated at a priced round comes with its own clean 83(b). Cost: a couple hours of lawyer time.

2. **Don't fix it, and commit to a bundle of things.** Not reporting ordinary comp income at your cliff and each monthly vest afterward. The company not withholding on that income. Signing the standard seed rep that all 83(b) elections were timely filed, knowing yours wasn't. Repeating that rep at A and B. Relying on nobody — seed counsel, A counsel, acquirer counsel — ever asking the question that's on their checklist. And accepting that if anyone does ask after the round prices, the free fix is gone and the expensive one (real income at acceleration, or exit recharacterization + company withholding liability) is what's left.

Option 2 isn't a "risk call" in the sense of a defensible position with some enforcement uncertainty. It's a decision to file inaccurate returns and make an inaccurate rep, and hope. You're allowed to make that decision; I'm just not going to call it something it isn't or help paper it.

**On your mentor:** "No one asked, we reported cap gains at exit" is a description of getting away with it, not of it being fine. And you don't actually know his facts — whether his shares vested, whether counsel quietly fixed it at seed, whether the buyer took an indemnity he didn't mention. Twenty exits without anyone ever requesting an 83(b) would be genuinely remarkable; it's the single most requested founder document in diligence.

The thing that gets me about this is the asymmetry. The fix costs you nothing today and stops costing nothing the day your round prices. If you want to take a gamble, at least take it after you've locked in the free option — accelerate the shares, let investors re-impose vesting with a proper 83(b), and then there's nothing left to gamble on.

Want me to draft the honest one-paragraph memo note plus a short board consent for the vesting acceleration? That's the version that actually gets counsel to say "noted" and move on.
